title: Preserving truth
hookLine: say "this is my belief", not "only this is true"

cards: Another sixteen-year-old brahmin, another tone entirely. His name is Kāpaṭhika, and he's sitting in a crowd around the Buddha with his elders, including the wealthy brahmin Caṅkī. He keeps interrupting.
The Buddha asks him to wait until the elders have finished. Caṅkī speaks up for him: he's learned, he can hold his own in a discussion. So the Buddha turns to him, and Kāpaṭhika asks a real question.
Our ancient hymns, he says, have been handed down for generations, and about them we brahmins conclude: only this is true, anything else is wrong. What do you say to that?

teach.b: The Buddha asks him: is there a single brahmin, now or in the past seven generations of teachers, who says, I know this, I see this: only this is true? No, Kāpaṭhika admits.

teach.h: FIVE WAYS OF HOLDING, EACH CAN GO TWO WAYS.
teach.b: Then, the Buddha says, it's like a line of blind people, each holding the one in front. The first doesn't see, the middle doesn't see, the last doesn't see.
Then he names five ways people come to hold things: faith, liking, tradition, careful reasoning, and a view that seems right after reflection. Each of these, he says, can turn out two ways.
Something deeply believed can be empty and false; something not believed at all can be true. So how does a person preserve the truth?
If a person has faith, they preserve the truth when they say: this is my faith.
And they don't go further, to the conclusion: only this is true, everything else is wrong. The same with liking, tradition, reasoning: this is what I've received, this is how I reason.
Said that way, the truth is kept safe. The Buddha doesn't tell Kāpaṭhika to drop his hymns. He tells him how to hold them honestly.
The sutta then goes on to discovering truth, and finally arriving at it, through long practice. But the first step is simply this way of speaking: say what you believe, and how you came to it.
That leaves room for the person across the table to do the same.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite this sutta, with the Kālāma Sutta, when encouraging students to hold teachings honestly, saying what they believe and why, and to verify through practice rather than insist on being right.

o: saying 'this is my faith' without claiming only it is true
guarding old hymns so not one word is ever changed
refusing to share a belief so it can't be challenged

games.q: how to preserve the truth: tap the pairs.
p: sixteen, asked about the ancient hymns
each holds the one in front
each can turn out two ways

s: the Buddha tells Kāpaṭhika to abandon his hymns
he tells him how to hold them honestly: this is my faith.
the sutta says something deeply believed can still be false
and something not believed at all can be true.
the Buddha asked the young man to wait, and Caṅkī spoke up for him
Caṅkī said he was learned and could hold his own; then the Buddha turned to his question.

games.q: you hold something by faith. how, in this sutta, do you preserve the truth when you speak of it?
games.why: 'this is my faith' keeps the truth safe; leaping to 'only this is true, everything else is wrong' does not.

practice: Bring one thing you hold strongly to mind and say it silently, the way you usually would, as a plain fact.
Then say it again with the Buddha's frame, this is my belief, or this is how I reason, and notice the difference in the body. Rest in the second way for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Preserving truth. Say this is my faith, this is how I reason, without leaping to only this is true. The Buddha's answer to a sixteen-year-old.

orig.note: Pali saccānurakkhaṇā: the preserving, or guarding, of truth.

carryVoice: Your line: preserve the truth. This is my faith, not only this is true. Week sixty-eight, done: vanna, Angulimāla, piya, the old king, iriyapatha, aggi, and preserving truth.
